doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Father's wedding bands, schnorrers and Naftule Brandwein
summary: Gibbs explains his father's Hasidic wedding bands with sidemen hired without music, clarinetist Naftule Brandwein, and the term schnorrer and the kishka story.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yes, okay. I want to start out, I’m not going to get through your whole life but there was a couple of things near the beginning of the book that really caught my attention, and one was your father’s — who hired sidemen — and you said some of them were “schnorrers”.

Well, my father taught schnorrers how to be classy musicians. He taught common people, common musicians, you know you’re talking about people who escaped from Russia like my father did — they all — and you know any musician my father ever hired it was like the Monday night Birdland jazz jam sessions where when you got there you were hired, you never really knew who you were going to play with — because no music, we all knew the same — we just played all the same songs. My father would have — he was a bandleader, and say he booked two weddings for a Saturday night. He’d have two different bands. My brother would be in charge of one and he’d be at the other, and the musicians that he hired, nobody knew who was going to show up at the job until they saw each other. And they all knew the music, I mean they were the best you could ever hear play what they call Hasidic music. No books, I mean these guys didn’t own books, what books? You know I hate to say when I hear young Jewish musicians playing with Jewish music, it’s fake. To me it’s fake. Because it’s almost like kids who go to school today come out and play jazz and they’re playing somebody else’s chorus or whatever it is. You know, they’re not being themselves. These musicians, it was ridiculous I mean how they were — when I was a young kid and playing with them — in fact I was just telling somebody there was a clarinet player called Naftule Brandwein, there’s a record he made in 1929 where he’s just playing clarinet and they’re all about like three minute songs and there’s about like twenty songs on this whole [inaudible]. I have the record somewhere, and I was going to send it to my friend, make a copy, because he was amazing. I worked with him, I wrote about him in my book, when I was about 16. He was an alcoholic. And my father would use him on the job but he made sure that he knew if he wanted to play

with my father he couldn’t be drunk on the job. But when he was a leader, and I played with him at 16 years old, you see what I wrote about him, I can’t say it on our show here, but you’ll see I wrote what he said to me.
He let me know I was rushing, but boy he just didn’t say you’re rushing you know.
A common person. It reminded me of, I spent a few years —
Half the people you grew up with, yeah.
Yeah, and people who would take things from the plate and take them home. Yeah, yeah.

Yeah. Especially there’s a Jewish dish called “kishka.” And it really was made the best at these catering halls. They made it so good that you wanted to go round to everybody’s plate after the job was over to see if they left it over, you’d put it in your pockets you know. My father taught them that, once again, if you want to be treated with class you’ve got to act like you have class. And that always remained with me you know.
